All the time that the eye took in these light appearances and the brain passed these light criticisms, there was in the heart a barbaric pity and fear which men have never been able to utter from the beginning, but which is the power behind half the poems of the world. The mood cannot even adequately be suggested, except faintly by this statement that tragedy is the highest expression of the infinite value of human life. Never had I stood so close to pain; and never so far away from pessimism. Ordinarily, I should not have spoken of these dark emotions at all, for speech about them is too difficult; but I mention them now for a specific and particular reason to the statement of which I will proceed at once. I speak these feelings because out of the furnace of them there came a curious realisation of a political or social truth. I saw with a queer and indescribable kind of clearness what a jury really is, and why we must never let it go.

The trend of our epoch up to this time has been consistently towards specialism and professionalism. We tend to have trained soldiers because they fight better, trained singers because they sing better, trained dancers because they dance better, specially instructed laughers because they laugh better, and so on and so on. The principle has been applied to law and politics by innumerable modern writers. Many Fabians have insisted that a greater part of our political work should be performed by experts. Many legalists have declared that the untrained jury should be altogether supplanted by the trained Judge.

.....

Now, if this world of ours were really what is called reasonable, I do not know that there would be any fault to find with this. But the true result of all experience and the true foundation of all religion is this. That the four or five things that it is most practically essential that a man should know, are all of them what people call paradoxes. That is to say, that though we all find them in life to be mere plain truths, yet we cannot easily state them in words without being guilty of seeming verbal contradictions. One of them, for instance, is the unimpeachable platitude that the man who finds most pleasure for himself is often the man who least hunts for it. Another is the paradox of courage; the fact that the way to avoid death is not to have too much aversion to it. Whoever is careless enough of his bones to climb some hopeful cliff above the tide may save his bones by that carelessness. Whoever will lose his life, the same shall save it; an entirely practical and prosaic statement.

message.content:
Throughout the moments in which the eye absorbed these luminous phenomena and the mind processed the associated reflections, there resided within the heart an instinctive compassion and dread—emotions that humanity has struggled to articulate since time immemorial, yet which serve as the driving force behind a significant portion of the world’s poetry. This sentiment is challenging to convey, but one might suggest that tragedy epitomizes the profound significance of human existence. Never had I been as close to anguish, nor had I felt as detached from despair. Typically, I would refrain from discussing such somber feelings, as articulating them proves complex; however, I bring them up now for a distinct reason that I will elaborate on immediately. These emotions emerged from a crucible of insight, leading to an unexpected understanding of a social or political reality. I glimpsed with a peculiar clarity the true nature of a jury and the imperative nature of its preservation.

Our current era has demonstrated a consistent movement toward specialization and professional expertise. We have cultivated skilled soldiers because they perform better in combat, trained singers due to their enhanced vocal abilities, and practiced dancers who execute their art with more finesse; the list is extensive. This principle of specialization has been echoed in the realms of law and politics by numerous contemporary thinkers. Many advocates of the Fabian society argue that a significant portion of political duties should be entrusted to experts. Similarly, a number of legal scholars have proposed that untrained jurors should be entirely replaced by expert judges.

If our world operated under the banner of reason, one might find little to criticize in this trend. Nevertheless, the essence of all experience and the crux of all faith reveals a profound truth: the essential knowledge that a person ought to possess often comprises what are deemed paradoxes. In other words, while we encounter these truths in our lives as straightforward realities, articulating them can lead to apparent verbal contradictions. For instance, it is a well-recognized truth that the individual who derives the most joy is frequently the one who does not actively pursue it. Another example is the paradox surrounding bravery; the notion that to evade death, one must not harbor an excessive fear of it. Those who are reckless enough to scale a promising cliff above the surf may protect themselves through that very recklessness. The adage, "whoever loses his life shall save it," is a statement that is both practical and profoundly grounded in reality.
